tagline: Africa's oldest republic, born of freedom
overview:
Liberia sits on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, between Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Ivory Coast, and is about the size of Tennessee. Its name means land of the free, because it was founded in the 1820s by freed African Americans, and its capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe. The flag, with red and white stripes and a single white star on blue, looks like a cousin of the American flag, and the country is Africa's oldest republic.

About 5.5 million people live in Liberia. English is the official language, spoken in a lively Liberian form, and about 20 local languages, including Kpelle, Bassa, and Mano, are spoken across the countryside. Most people are Christian, with a Muslim minority. Liberia is a presidential republic that has held peaceful elections since two devastating civil wars ended in 2003. Rubber plantations, iron ore, and gold are the main exports, and Liberia's flag flies on thousands of ships worldwide because the country lets foreign shipowners register vessels there.
landAndNature: Liberia's coast is a line of sandy beaches, lagoons, and mangrove swamps pounded by Atlantic surf, backed by rolling hills and dense tropical rainforest. It holds a large share of the remaining Upper Guinea rainforest, one of the wettest and richest forests in Africa, with Sapo National Park at its heart. Forest elephants, chimpanzees, and the pygmy hippo, a shy nighttime animal about the size of a large pig, live there, along with rare zebra duikers and colorful hornbills. The land rises to the Nimba range in the north, where Mount Wuteve reaches about 1,440 meters. Rivers such as the St. Paul, St. John, and Cavalla flow to the sea. Liberia is one of the rainiest countries in Africa, with Monrovia getting about five meters of rain a year.
peopleAndCulture: Liberians belong to peoples such as the Kpelle, Bassa, Grebo, Gio, Mano, and Kru, plus the Americo-Liberians descended from the founders, and Liberian English blends all of these into a colorful spoken style. Rice is eaten at almost every meal, with palm butter, cassava leaf, or pepper soup, along with fufu and fried plantains. Secret societies called Poro and Sande have long taught young people traditions in the forest. Music mixes local rhythms with gospel and hipco, a Liberian hip-hop sung in local English. Soccer is the top sport, and George Weah, the only African player ever named world player of the year, went on to become president. Independence Day on July 26 is celebrated with parades and dancing.
history: Peoples such as the Kpelle and Kru lived here for centuries before the American Colonization Society began settling freed Black Americans on the coast in 1822. The settlers declared the independent Republic of Liberia on July 26, 1847, with a constitution modeled on the United States, but for over a century they ruled over the indigenous majority, who had few rights. A US rubber company set up huge plantations in 1926. A coup in 1980 led by Samuel Doe ended Americo-Liberian rule, and civil wars from 1989 to 2003 killed about 250,000 people and destroyed the country. Women's peace protests helped end the fighting. In 2005 Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected female president, and she later shared the Nobel Peace Prize. An Ebola outbreak in 2014 and 2015 killed thousands.
funFacts: Liberia's capital, Monrovia, is one of only two capitals in the world named after a US president; the other is Washington, D.C.
Liberia was the first African country to elect a woman president, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, in 2005.
The pygmy hippo lives almost only in Liberia's forests and is so shy it was unknown to Western science until the 1840s.
More ships are registered under Liberia's flag than almost any other country, even though few of them ever visit Liberia.
Liberia and Ethiopia were the only African nations that remained independent throughout the colonial era.
